title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling, Benchmarks, Runbooks
author: Priya Khanna
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbook, benchmarking suite, release notes highlights, known issues, and operational runbooks used by the Serving Runtime team. It is intended as the canonical reference for on-call engineers, benchmarking owners, and platform product managers.

Key goals
- Provide a single-source-of-truth for runtime behaviour, supported configurations, and troubleshooting steps.
- Standardize profiling and benchmarking procedures so performance regressions are measurable and actionable.
- Document kernel scheduling and placement policies that trade off latency, throughput, and cost.

Audience and scope
- Primary audience: serving-runtime engineers, SRE, bench team, performance reviewers, and partner infra teams.
- Scope: inference-serving runtime (gRPC/HTTP frontend, dispatcher, scheduler, GPU workers, KV cache service, autoscaling). Not covered: client SDKs, model training pipelines, or Dedicated pod provisioning flows (see related deployment docs).

1) Runtime Architecture (high level)

Summary diagram (text):
- API Gateway (hosted) -> Frontend (HTTP/gRPC) -> Request Router -> Scheduler/Dispatcher -> Worker Pool (GPU pods) -> KV Cache / State DB -> Metrics & Tracing Collector

Key services and ownership
- frontend-service: HTTP/gRPC terminating proxy, request validation, and auth (owner: frontend team).
- router-service: smart routing, region/capacity policy, and model-variant fallbacks (owner: runtime-core).
- scheduler-service: kernel selection, worker assignment, batching policy enforcement (owner: runtime-core).
- worker-runtime: per-GPU process running compiled kernels and managing KV cache + quantized model shards (owner: serving-runtime).
- kv-cache: redis-backed prefix cache (owner: infra-cache).
- metrics-collector: Prometheus + tracing exporter to Tempo (owner: observability).

SLOs and thresholds (service-level)
- End-to-end P95 latency (text-generation, seq_len=128): 120ms for small models (<=2B), 400ms for medium models (2B-20B), 1200ms for large models (>20B).
- Availability (99.95% monthly for hosted tier).
- Request error rate: <0.1% (5xx from runtime).
- Cold-start SLA for private/dedicated: warm worker spin-up < 30s.

Deployment topology notes
- Worker pools are labeled by model-variant, quantization profile (int8/fp16), and GPU type (A100/H100).
- Autoscaling decisions use a dual metric: effective token throughput and pending-batch latency. If pending-batch latency > 50ms for 30s, scale-up trigger fires.

2) Kernel scheduling and placement

Design summary
- Purpose: select kernel implementations and map incoming token-generation work across GPU resources to meet latency SLOs while maximizing throughput and hardware utilization.
- Two-level decision: (a) kernel variant selection (fast-approx, precise) based on model and input length distribution; (b) placement across worker shards and per-GPU streams.

Policies
- Latency-first mode (default for hosted free-tier): prefer low-latency kernels even if throughput drops by up to 20%.
- Cost-first mode (customer-configurable for Dedicated): prefer high-throughput kernels and batching to reduce per-token cost, with configurable latency max (e.g., p95 <= 300ms).
- Mixed mode for tiered routing: short-tail requests routed to latency-first pool, long-chat sessions to cost-first.

Kernel selection rules (examples)
- For attention: use fused attention-kernel-v3 for seq_len <= 512 on H100; fallback to block-attn-v1 for >2048 tokens.
- For MLP matmuls: prefer tensor-core-quantized kernels when model uses int8 quantization profile.

Example kernel-config snippet (YAML, used by scheduler):

kernel_policies:
  - model_family: "vicuna*"
    conditions:
      - max_seq: 512
      - quantization: "int8"
    preferred_kernel: "attn-fused-v3"
    fallback_kernels: ["attn-block-v1", "attn-host-fallback"]

Performance counters and telemetry
- Per-worker metrics exposed: kernel_exec_ms, queue_wait_ms, batch_size_histogram, kv_cache_hit_rate. These feed alerts and autoscaling decisions.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to run a standard profile)

When to profile
- Before/after a kernel change, scheduler tweak, or model quantization upgrade. Also for post-incident deep-dive when P95 latency increases persistently.

Tools and environment
- perf-infer (internal wrapper around pytorch profiler / Nsight).
- metrics-exporter: /metrics endpoint and tracing via OTLP.
- nvprof/nsys for GPU-level traces (only used in gated environment where HSM keys permit).

Step-by-step profiling checklist
1. Reproduce workload: use benchctl to replay the production-like trace for at least 5 minutes. Command example:
   benchctl replay --trace-id <trace-id> --concurrency 50 --seq-len-dist "short:0.6,medium:0.3,long:0.1" --output profile-run.json
2. Enable profiler and set sampling: perf-infer profile --target worker://gpu-1 --duration 300 --mode "kernel+memory" --out /tmp/prof-$(date +%s).nsys
3. Collect traces and perf counters: curl http://worker-1.local:9000/metrics > worker-metrics.prom
4. Upload artifacts to perf-bucket and open the perf dashboard:
   gsutil cp /tmp/prof-*.nsys gs://redwood-perf/profiles/$(date +%Y%m%d)/
5. Annotate and link in the profiling ticket with key observations: heavy queue_wait_ms, specific kernel hot-spot, or memory stall.

Interpreting results (common signals)
- long queue_wait_ms + small kernel_exec_ms: insufficient batching/underutilized GPU. Consider switching to cost-first policy or increasing batch window by 10ms increments.
- high kernel_exec_ms with high tensor-core utilization: expected; check if kernel variant is optimal for model shape.
- KV cache miss spikes: verify prefix caching policy and cache ttl.

4) Benchmarking suite (standard tests and metrics)

Benchmark goals
- Measure token throughput (tokens/s), token cost (tokens/$), and latency percentiles across model families, quantization profiles, and hardware types.

Standard test matrix
- Model families: small (Llama-2 7B), medium (Llama-2 13B), large (Llama-3 70B).
- Quantization: fp16, int8, int8-mixed.
- Hardware: A100-80GB, H100-80GB.
- Load profiles: single-shot short (seq=64), batched short (batch=16, seq=128), streaming multi-step (session of 200 tokens).

Canonical benchmark command
- benchctl run --model llama-2-13b --quant int8 --gpu h100 --load single-shot --duration 600 --out results.json

Metrics we store (per-run)
- avg_tokens_per_second, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, cost_per_1k_tokens_usd, batch_size_histogram

Sample results (excerpt)
- llama-2-13b int8 H100 single-shot: avg_tokens_per_second=1200, p95_latency_ms=380, cost_per_1k_tokens_usd=0.28
- llama-3-70b fp16 A100 batched(16): avg_tokens_per_second=2100, p95_latency_ms=1250, cost_per_1k_tokens_usd=1.14

Regression detection
- Every benchmark run is compared against baseline in the perf-regression index. A >7% regression in p95 or >10% increase in cost_per_1k triggers an automatic regression ticket and assigns to the model-onboarding + runtime teams.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)

2026-02-10 Release 2026.2.10 (runtime-core)
- Kernel: added attn-fused-v3 with 15-22% p95 improvement for seq<=512 on H100.
- Scheduler: introduced per-request latency budget metadata; router can now route by latency budget.
- Profiling: perf-infer added automated nsys trace diffing.

Backports and rollouts
- attn-fused-v3 enabled as opt-in for Dedicated on 2026-02-18; auto-enabled on hosted region-us-1 on 2026-02-25 after soak.

6) Known issues (operational)

Active issues as of 2026-03-04:
- Issue RUNTIME-4123: intermittent 5xx from worker-runtime when large model >64k context is requested. Root cause: pagination of KV cache indexing causing OOM during lookup. Mitigation: reject requests >50k tokens with 413 and provide client guidance. Owner: serving-runtime.
- Issue RUNTIME-4051: slow warmup on small H100 clusters after maintenance windows causing P95 spikes for 10-15 minutes. Mitigation: pre-warm workers using warmup-ctl (see runbook). Owner: eng-sre.
- Issue RUNTIME-3987: occasional quantization mismatch for int8-mixed profile when upgrading kernel package 2.12. Workaround: pin kernel image to 2.10 for affected customers. Owner: runtime-core.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

Runbook: P95 latency regression (first response)
1. Triage: look at grafana dashboard 'runtime/p95-latency' last 1 hour and check which model-family and region is affected.
2. If error rate > 0.5% escalate to page on-call (pager: #runtime-oncall).
3. Confirm whether regression coincides with a recent deployment (check deploy-log for the last 30m).
4. Run quick profile on representative worker: perf-infer sample --worker worker-12 --duration 60
5. If queue_wait_ms is top contributor increase scale-by +20% or switch routing to latency-first pool.
6. Open incident ticket with summary, attach profile artifacts and assign to runtime-core.

Runbook: Worker OOM due to KV cache (RUNTIME-4123)
1. Identify worker pod: kubectl get pods -l app=worker-runtime -o wide --field-selector status.phase=CrashLoopBackOff
2. kubectl logs <pod> --previous and grep for "KV_LOOKUP_OOM"
3. If confirmed, set kv-cache-ttl to 30s for the model via API: curl -X POST "https://config-service.internal/v1/models/<model>/cache" -d '{"ttl_s":30}'
4. Scale down traffic to the model via router: routerctl route update --model <model> --weight 0.2
5. Owner: serving-runtime to produce fix.

Runbook: Pre-warm after maintenance
1. Run warmup-ctl prewarm --pool <pool-id> --target 20 --model-family "llama*"
2. Monitor 'worker_ready' metric and ensure warmup completes within 10m.

Appendix: Useful commands and snippets
- Check P95 by model: curl -s "https://metrics-api.internal/v1/query?metric=p95_latency&model=llama-2-13b&window=5m" | jq
- Run a benchmark: benchctl run --model "llama-2-7b" --quant fp16 --gpu a100 --load batched --duration 300
- Profile worker: perf-infer profile --target worker://gpu-24 --mode kernel+queues --duration 180 --out /tmp/out.nsight
